module.title: Summations
module.description: Module 6 covers SUMMATIONS: ∑ notation (index, lower and upper bounds, summand), the basic summation rules (constant factor, sum of a constant, linearity, splitting), the four standard CLOSED-FORM formulas (∑1 = n, ∑i = n(n+1)/2, ∑i² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, ∑i³ = (n(n+1)/2)²), and the FINITE GEOMETRIC SERIES formula. Together these are the techniques you need to evaluate almost any sum that appears in CPCS222.

lessons.title: Summation Notation and Basic Rules
lessons.welcome: Welcome to Module 6. Adding up the terms of a sequence is so common that mathematicians invented a compact notation: the BIG SIGMA ∑. In this lesson you will learn how to read and write a summation, identify each piece (index, bounds, summand), and apply the BASIC RULES that let you transform and simplify sums BEFORE plugging in values: pulling out constants, splitting a summand by linearity, and adjusting the bounds with the splitting rule.
objectives: Read and write a summation in ∑ notation, identifying the index, lower bound, upper bound, and summand.
Unroll a small sum to its explicit '+' form by hand.
Apply the constant-factor rule: pull out a factor that does not depend on the index.
Apply the sum-of-a-constant rule: ∑_{i=1}^{n} k = kn.
Apply linearity to split a sum-of-sums and the splitting rule to change bounds.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: It is shorthand for 1² + 2² + 3² + 4² + 5². The i is the INDEX, 1 is the LOWER bound, 5 is the UPPER bound, and i² is the SUMMAND.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Can I just multiply through if there's a constant factor?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Yes — if it does not depend on the index. ∑ 5·i = 5·∑ i because 5 stays outside every term. But you cannot pull i out of ∑ i² because i changes each step.

sections.heading: Reading a Summation
sections.explanation:
The summation

  ∑_{i=m}^{n} f(i)

means f(m) + f(m+1) + f(m+2) + ⋯ + f(n). The four ingredients:

  • i — the INDEX (a temporary variable).
  • m — the LOWER BOUND.
  • n — the UPPER BOUND.
  • f(i) — the SUMMAND.

If n < m, the sum is EMPTY by convention and equals 0. The choice of letter for the index is arbitrary — i, j, k all work — but be consistent inside one expression.
common_mistakes: Off-by-one on bounds. ∑_{i=1}^{n} has n terms; ∑_{i=0}^{n} has n+1 terms.
Reusing the index letter for two different roles in nested sums.

visual_idea.description: An animated 'unrolled' view: the ∑ on the left morphs term-by-term into the explicit sum on the right, one + sign appearing per index step.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Drag the upper bound slider to add or remove terms from the unrolled sum live.

sections.heading: Constant-Factor Rule
sections.explanation:
If c does not depend on the index, you may PULL it OUT of the sum:

  ∑_{i=m}^{n} c · f(i)  =  c · ∑_{i=m}^{n} f(i).

Watch out: only EXPRESSIONS THAT DO NOT DEPEND ON THE INDEX may be pulled out. You can pull out 5 from ∑ 5·i, but you cannot pull out i from ∑ i·f(i) because i changes with each term.
examples: Cannot pull out i from ∑ i · 2ⁱ — i is not constant.
common_mistakes: Pulling out a factor that depends on the index. Always check whether the expression contains the index variable.
Forgetting that the constant multiplies the WHOLE SUM, not each individual term separately.

visual_idea.description: Animation of a '5' factor crossing the ∑ sign: shown shrinking inside the sum, then ballooning outside as an external multiplier.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Try to drag 'i' outside the ∑; the page rejects it with 'depends on the index'.

sections.heading: Sum of a Constant
sections.explanation:
If the SUMMAND itself is a constant k (no index appearing), the sum just counts how many times k is added:

  ∑_{i=m}^{n} k  =  k · (n − m + 1).

Special case: ∑_{i=1}^{n} k = k · n, and ∑_{i=1}^{n} 1 = n.

This rule combines with the constant-factor rule to simplify many sums in two quick steps.
common_mistakes: Treating ∑_{i=1}^{n} k as just k. The constant is summed n times, not once.
Off-by-one when the lower bound is not 1. The count of terms is (n − m + 1), not (n − m).

visual_idea.description: A row of identical k's, one per index value. The total at the right multiplies k by the number of cells.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Slide both bounds m and n; the count of cells updates and the formula k(n − m + 1) is displayed.

sections.heading: Linearity (Sum of a Sum)
sections.explanation:
Sums distribute over addition:

  ∑_{i=m}^{n} (f(i) + g(i))  =  ∑_{i=m}^{n} f(i) + ∑_{i=m}^{n} g(i).

And subtraction:

  ∑_{i=m}^{n} (f(i) − g(i))  =  ∑_{i=m}^{n} f(i) − ∑_{i=m}^{n} g(i).

Combined with the constant-factor rule, this gives FULL LINEARITY:

  ∑ (a · f(i) + b · g(i))  =  a · ∑ f(i) + b · ∑ g(i).
common_mistakes: Trying to use linearity over multiplication. ∑(f(i) · g(i)) ≠ ∑f(i) · ∑g(i) in general.
Forgetting to apply linearity also to constant terms; ∑(f(i) + 5) splits into ∑f(i) + 5n.

visual_idea.description: A pipeline showing a single ∑ over (f + g) splitting into two separate ∑ symbols joined by +.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Toggle 'add a constant term' and watch the new ∑ k → kn term appear.

sections.heading: Changing the Lower Bound — The Splitting Rule
sections.explanation:
Sometimes the closed-form formulas you'll meet in Lesson 2 require a lower bound of 1 or 0. To use them with a different lower bound, SHIFT or SPLIT:

  ∑_{i=m}^{n} f(i)  =  ∑_{i=1}^{n} f(i)  −  ∑_{i=1}^{m-1} f(i).

This splits the [m, n] range into [1, n] minus [1, m-1]. Both pieces use a lower bound of 1, ready for the standard formulas.
common_mistakes: Subtracting ∑_{i=1}^{m} instead of ∑_{i=1}^{m-1}. The split removes one fewer term than the new lower bound.
Failing to shift before applying the closed-form formulas, leading to off-by-one errors.

visual_idea.description: A horizontal range bar from 1 to n; the user slides a marker to position m and the bar splits into '[1, m−1]' (subtracted) and '[m, n]' (kept).
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Hover the split point to see the formula instantiated with current m and n.

step_by_step_solution: Apply the sum-of-a-constant rule with k = 5 and (n − 1 + 1) = n terms.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Adding the constant 5 a total of n times.

worked_examples.problem: Use linearity and the constant rule to simplify ∑_{i=1}^{n} (3 + 2i) without yet using closed forms.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Two independent transformations break the sum into ready-to-evaluate pieces.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to apply ∑3 = 3n; some students stop too early at ∑3.

worked_examples.problem: Use the splitting rule: rewrite ∑_{i=4}^{12} f(i) using bounds starting at 1.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Splitting [4, 12] = [1, 12] minus [1, 3] keeps both pieces in standard form.

∑_{i=1}^{n} 4 =
quick_checks.explanation: Sum of n copies of the constant 4.

quick_checks.question: You can pull out the index variable i from ∑ i · f(i).
quick_checks.explanation: Only constants (expressions independent of the index) can be pulled out.

key_takeaways: Pull constants OUT of sums when the factor doesn't depend on the index.
∑_{i=m}^{n} k = k(n − m + 1); special case ∑_{i=1}^{n} 1 = n.
summary.next: Next we meet the four CLOSED-FORM formulas for the most common summands (1, i, i², i³) and the geometric series — your fastest route from a long sum to a single number.

lessons.title: Closed-Form Formulas and the Geometric Series
lessons.welcome: Now that you can manipulate summations with the basic rules, it is time to turn long sums into instant answers. Four CLOSED-FORM formulas — for ∑1, ∑i, ∑i², ∑i³ — appear over and over throughout the rest of the course. Add the GEOMETRIC SERIES formula and you have a small but extremely powerful library that handles most sums you'll meet in CPCS222.
objectives: State and apply the four standard closed forms: ∑1 = n, ∑i = n(n+1)/2, ∑i² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, ∑i³ = (n(n+1)/2)².
State and apply the finite geometric series formula ∑_{i=0}^{n} a·rⁱ = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1.
Combine basic rules with closed forms to evaluate compound sums in a few lines.
Recognize when r = 1 forces a special-case treatment of the geometric series.
Evaluate sums with shifted lower bounds using the splitting rule from Lesson 1.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Is there a faster way than computing each term in ∑_{i=1}^{100} i?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Yes — the Gauss formula: n(n+1)/2. With n = 100 that gives 100·101/2 = 5050. One line.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: It equals the square of ∑i. Cubes pile up to a perfect square — striking and worth remembering.

sections.heading: Four Closed-Form Formulas to Memorize
sections.explanation:
These four formulas appear throughout the course. Burn them into your memory.

  ∑_{i=1}^{n} 1   =  n
  ∑_{i=1}^{n} i   =  n(n + 1) / 2
  ∑_{i=1}^{n} i²  =  n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6
  ∑_{i=1}^{n} i³  =  (n(n + 1) / 2)²  =  ( ∑_{i=1}^{n} i )²

All four assume the index starts at 1. For lower bound 0 or other values, use the splitting rule from Lesson 1.

Mnemonics:
  • ∑i is Gauss's formula — pair the first with the last, second with second-last, and so on.
  • ∑i³ is the SQUARE of ∑i. Striking, easy to remember.
common_mistakes: Confusing ∑i and ∑i² formulas. Practice writing them out from scratch a few times.
Off-by-one when the lower bound is 0. Most formulas assume i = 1 to n; adjust if i starts at 0.

visual_idea.description: Four reference cards laid out side by side. Each card shows the formula, a small numerical example (n = 5 or 10), and a tiny picture (1+2+…+n as a triangle, etc.).
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click any card to flip it and see a quick proof or intuition (Gauss pairing for ∑i; column-stacking argument for ∑i²).

sections.heading: The Finite Geometric Series
sections.explanation:
A finite geometric series sums the first n + 1 terms of a geometric progression:

  ∑_{i=0}^{n} a · rⁱ  =  a · (rⁿ⁺¹ − 1) / (r − 1),  for r ≠ 1.

When r = 1 every term equals a, so the sum is (n + 1) · a — handle this case separately to avoid division by zero.

If |r| < 1, letting n → ∞ gives the INFINITE GEOMETRIC SERIES:

  ∑_{i=0}^{∞} a · rⁱ  =  a / (1 − r)   for |r| < 1.

Geometric sums show up in compound interest, discounting cash flows, and analyzing recursive algorithms.
common_mistakes: Using the formula when r = 1 — division by zero. Handle r = 1 separately.
Off-by-one in the exponent. Note rⁿ⁺¹, not rⁿ, when summing i = 0 to n.

visual_idea.description: Bars representing terms a, ar, ar², …, arⁿ. Total height equals the closed-form value; sliding n changes the number of bars.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Slide r between 0 and 2 and watch the bars stretch or shrink; the total updates live.

sections.heading: A Strategy for Combined Sums
sections.explanation:
Most sums you'll meet combine several rules and formulas. Strategy:

  1. PULL OUT constants (Lesson 1).
  2. SPLIT the summand using linearity if it has multiple terms.
  3. SHIFT bounds using the splitting rule if needed.
  4. APPLY closed-form formulas to each piece.
  5. SIMPLIFY the resulting algebra.

With practice, what looks like a long sum collapses into a few lines of work.
common_mistakes: Applying closed forms before pulling out constants — leading to algebra mistakes.

visual_idea.description: A pipeline: input → 'pull constants' → 'split summand' → 'apply closed forms' → 'simplify' → final answer. Each box editable with a worked-step display.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Type a sum; the page walks the pipeline live and shows the output at each stage.

worked_examples.common_mistake: Computing 50·51 wrong; arithmetic is the bottleneck once the formula is right.

worked_examples.why_it_works: Linearity splits the sum; the two closed forms handle each piece.
Direct application of the finite geometric series formula.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using rⁿ instead of rⁿ⁺¹ in the numerator. With indices 0 to n there are n + 1 terms.

worked_examples.why_it_works: Closed-form formulas assume index starts at 1; the splitting rule handles arbitrary lower bounds.

quick_checks.question: Is ∑_{i=0}^{n} a·rⁱ = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1) valid for r = 1?
quick_checks.explanation: When r = 1, the denominator vanishes; handle r = 1 as a separate case (sum = (n+1)·a).

quick_checks.question: ∑i³ = (∑i)².
quick_checks.explanation: Sum of cubes equals the square of the sum: n²(n+1)²/4 = (n(n+1)/2)².

key_takeaways: When r = 1, the geometric sum simplifies to (n+1)·a.
Strategy: pull constants → split → shift bounds → apply closed forms → simplify.
These five formulas, plus the rules from Lesson 1, handle most sums you'll meet in CPCS222.
summary.next: You now have a complete toolkit for summation. Move to the Module 6 exercises to practice fluently.

exercises.title: Module 6 Exercises — Summations
exercises.description: Practice problems covering summation notation, basic summation rules (constant factor, sum of a constant, linearity, splitting), the four standard closed-form formulas, and the geometric series.

questions.question: How many terms are in ∑_{i=3}^{10} f(i)?
∑_{i=1}^{n} 5 =
questions.explanation: Sum of n copies of the constant 5.

questions.question: ∑_{i=1}^{n} (2i − 1) =
questions.explanation: Sum of first n odd numbers is n².

questions.question: ∑_{i=1}^{n} c = cn for any constant c.
questions.explanation: Adding c a total of n times.

questions.question: ∑_{i=1}^{n} (f(i)·g(i)) = (∑f(i))·(∑g(i)).
questions.explanation: Linearity does NOT distribute over multiplication.

questions.question: ∑_{i=1}^{n} i³ = (n(n+1)/2)².
questions.explanation: Sum of cubes equals square of sum of integers.

questions.question: The geometric formula a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1) is valid when r = 1.
questions.explanation: r = 1 makes the denominator zero; use (n + 1)·a instead.

questions.question: You can pull the index variable i out of ∑ i·f(i).
questions.explanation: Only constants (no index dependence) can be pulled out.

questions.question: Why is ∑_{i=0}^{n} a·rⁱ = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1) only valid for r ≠ 1?
questions.answer: When r = 1, the denominator is 0. In that case every term equals a, so the sum is (n + 1)·a.
questions.explanation: Always handle r = 1 as a separate case.

questions.question: Apply the splitting rule: rewrite ∑_{i=5}^{20} i² in terms of ∑_{i=1}^{20} i² and another sum.
Compute ∑_{i=1}^{n} (5 − 2i) using basic rules and closed forms.
questions.explanation: Linearity, constant rule, ∑i closed form, simplify.

questions.question: What is the cardinality interpretation of ∑_{i=1}^{n} 1?
questions.answer: It counts how many terms are in the sum — namely n. Equivalently, |{1, 2, …, n}| = n.

questions.question: Why does linearity NOT distribute over multiplication?
questions.answer: ∑(f·g) sums the product f(i)·g(i) for each i, while (∑f)(∑g) multiplies the totals. The two are usually different. Example: f(i) = g(i) = 1 for n = 2 gives ∑(f·g) = 2 but (∑f)(∑g) = 4.

questions.question: Evaluate ∑_{i=1}^{20} (i² + 3i + 2).
questions.explanation: Three closed forms plus simple arithmetic.

questions.question: Show ∑_{i=1}^{n} i(i+1) = n(n+1)(n+2)/3 by expanding and using closed forms.
An infinite geometric series has a = 1 and r = 1/3. Compute its sum and compare to the partial sum at n = 4.

questions.instructions: Pull constants, split, apply ∑i = n(n+1)/2, ∑i² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, ∑i³ = (n(n+1)/2)², or geometric formula as appropriate.
